key_insight: This paper shows that a two-stage stacking model can combine patient-reported outcomes with clinical data to better identify head and neck cancer survivors at risk of dysphagia. The approach aims to make late-toxicity surveillance more practical by reducing reliance on specialized swallow imaging.
problem_solved: Routine dysphagia screening in head and neck cancer survivorship is difficult because the gold-standard assessment, videofluoroscopy-based CTCAE-DIGEST, is costly, resource-intensive, and burdensome for patients. The paper addresses the need for a scalable way to stratify risk earlier and more efficiently.
method: Use patient-reported outcomes (PROs) as a low-burden signal for swallowing-related symptoms.
Combine PROs with clinical variables in a two-stage stacking framework to improve risk prediction.
Train a model to stratify patients into dysphagia risk groups without requiring routine imaging for every survivor.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this is a strong example of multimodal clinical risk modeling with practical deployment constraints in mind. It highlights how stacking and PRO-based features can extend predictive care beyond expensive gold-standard tests.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing PROs and clinical data feeding into a two-stage stacking model
Risk stratification funnel or traffic-light chart for low/medium/high dysphagia risk
Comparison graphic of gold-standard videofluoroscopy vs. model-based screening
Icons representing patient survey, clinic data, and swallowing assessment
paper_title: Dysphagia Risk Stratification in Head and Neck Cancer via Two-Stage PRO-Clinical Stacking
paper_authors: Siyuan Zhao, Eric Ababio Anyimadu, Zachary G. Brumm, Yue Ma, Clifton David Fuller
